intro: Bach gives flute, violin and harpsichord solo roles, then leaves the keyboard alone for an extended written-out cadenza. How does the balance change when one player supplies melody, bass and harmony?
question: How does the harpsichord take over the concerto?

relations.label: The opening ritornello returns
relations.basis: The opening and final ritornellos frame the solo episodes and written-out cadenza; the section map places the final tutti near 568 s. CENS diagonal mean 0.954, sustained 17 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 566.5 s (cache/form/bach-brandenburg-5-allegro.txt, candidate 2; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: A recurring orchestral frame
cues.text: The opening establishes the D major ritornello: ensemble music that returns between solo episodes. Keep its coordinated rhythm in mind as the solo writing becomes more independent.
cues.evidence: The concerto’s score establishes the ritornello design; this note describes the opening passage, not a timed entrance.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Three instruments in conversation
cues.text: Flute, violin and harpsichord form the solo group. Compare the keyboard’s short, plucked notes with the longer lines available to the flute and violin; the harpsichord has a written-out solo part, not just accompanying chords.
cues.evidence: The 1721 score names these three solo instruments; the recording analysis cannot identify their individual entrances.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A month in confinement
cues.text: Bach accepted the Köthen court’s offer in 1717 before obtaining permission to leave Weimar. His employer had him confined for almost a month. Only after his dismissal could he take up the new post with Prince Leopold.
cues.evidence: Bach-Archiv Leipzig’s chronology records the contract, imprisonment and dismissal under 1717.

cues.title: Beyond the home key
cues.text: In these solo episodes, listen for a familiar rhythmic pattern continuing as the harmony changes. A sequence repeats a short musical shape at another pitch, allowing continuity without staying in one key.
cues.evidence: This is a listening guide to sequential writing, not a claim that a particular modulation occurs at this time.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A dedication, not a premiere
cues.text: Bach dated the presentation manuscript of the six concertos 24 March 1721 and dedicated it to Christian Ludwig, Margrave of Brandenburg. That date does not establish when the Fifth Concerto was first performed.
cues.evidence: The dedication is dated 24 March 1721; the concerto also survives in an earlier version, BWV 1050.1.

cues.title: Less level, continuing motion
cues.text: Through this stretch, compare the rapid internal movement with the quieter overall sound. A passage can contain many separate attacks without carrying the weight of a full ensemble statement.
cues.evidence: The measured relative level falls across 3:15–3:40 while detected attacks remain frequent; this does not identify which instruments are playing.

cues.title: A stronger stretch
cues.text: The surrounding passage grows substantially in level. Listen for whether the rhythmic figures become easier to hear together as the sound strengthens, rather than assuming that a stronger sound means faster notes.
cues.evidence: Relative level rises by about 9 dB between 3:55 and 4:10; the analysis places a change near 3:56.

cues.title: Köthen to Leipzig
cues.text: Bach served Prince Leopold at Köthen before taking up the Leipzig cantor’s post in 1723. In Leipzig, his duties included cantatas for Sundays and feast days: a different institutional setting from the court that employed him when he dedicated these concertos.
cues.evidence: Bach-Archiv Leipzig’s chronology documents the Köthen appointment in 1717 and the Leipzig duties from 1723.

cues.title: The later coffeehouse concerts
cues.text: From 1729 Bach directed Leipzig’s Collegium Musicum at Café Zimmermann. Its concerts included his orchestral suites and violin and harpsichord concertos, providing an instrumental platform outside the church service.
cues.evidence: Bach-Archiv Leipzig’s 1729 chronology entry identifies the venue and the repertoire.

cues.title: An extended keyboard solo
cues.text: The extended cadenza is the movement’s largest change of scale: one harpsichord supplies the whole texture. Across this solo, listen for a bass line beneath the running notes rather than treating every quick figure as a separate melody.
cues.evidence: The score contains a long solo cadenza; the sustained lower-level sound from roughly 6:25 to 9:25 supports this approximate placement.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A composed display
cues.text: Bach writes out the cadenza rather than leaving an empty space for improvisation. Follow how its figures distribute melody and accompaniment between the two hands; rapid notes can prolong a harmony as well as change it.
cues.evidence: The written-out harpsichord cadenza is present in the score; no individual figure is aligned to this recording.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Remember the ensemble rhythm
cues.text: During the later part of the cadenza, keep the opening ritornello in mind. Its eventual return will restore several players moving together after the keyboard’s unaccompanied passage.
cues.evidence: The score places the final ritornello after the cadenza; the analysis supports a broad transition around 9:25–9:30, not an entrance time.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The closing ritornello
cues.text: The closing passage restores the orchestral ritornello after the long keyboard solo. Compare its coordinated rhythm with the opening: the concerto ends by re-establishing the ensemble rather than extending the solo display.
cues.evidence: The score supplies the formal return; rising relative level around 9:25–9:35 supports the passage’s approximate location.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: From cadence to quiet
cues.text: The ending moves from the ensemble’s final cadence into a short tail of residual sound. Follow the decay rather than expecting another solo episode.
cues.evidence: The measured relative level falls by about 47 dB between the 9:45 and 9:50 analysis windows.

transitions.title: The cadence opens a conversation
transitions.how: The opening ritornello closes in D major, but its regular pulse continues into the solo episode. Flute and solo violin exchange short figures above the harpsichord’s running part; the keyboard still supplies a bass as well as an independent upper line. Bach reduces the ensemble rather than changing tempo. Sequential repetition then carries the conversation towards A major, the dominant: the same small figures can continue while their harmonic destination changes.
transitions.evidence: The section boundary is 0:22; the analysis detects a boundary there and D-centred sound followed by an A-major region around 0:35–0:50. The written eight-bar opening ritornello and first solo episode supply the cadence, scoring and key route; the SFCM form chart places the next ritornello in the dominant: https://sfcm.edu/sites/default/files/sfcm-theory/analysis_lectures/21_concerto/brandenburg_5_chart.pdf. No individual entrance is aligned.

transitions.title: The bass stays with the keyboard
transitions.how: As the other players withdraw, the harpsichord keeps both the bass and the moving upper parts. The departure is not into a new tempo or a new theme: Bach enlarges the keyboard figuration already present in the solo episodes. A major, the dominant of D, becomes the cadenza’s principal harmonic ground. Sequences and increasingly rapid divisions postpone the return to D while one player assumes the functions of soloist and accompanying ensemble.
transitions.evidence: The map places the cadenza at 6:26, also a measured structural boundary. Relative level falls from −14.8 dB at 6:20 to −21.2 dB at 6:25, while brightness rises; this supports a change of texture, not instrument identification. Bach’s written-out cadenza begins at bar 154 and prolongs the dominant before bar 219; see the SFCM chart cited above. The boundary remains approximate.

transitions.title: A bass pedal releases the tutti
transitions.how: Near the end of the cadenza, A in the bass anchors the keyboard’s rapid figuration: a dominant pedal keeps the promised D major waiting while the upper notes crowd around it. The final ritornello releases that pressure into the tonic. Strings restore the opening’s coordinated rhythmic figure, and the harpsichord rejoins the ensemble texture instead of continuing its unaccompanied display. The decisive change is from one player’s divided hands to several parts articulating the familiar ritornello together.
transitions.evidence: The final-ritornello boundary is 9:28. Analysis shows the lower-level keyboard region giving way to a rise from 9:25–9:35 and D-major estimates after 9:30. The score supplies the closing dominant pedal and tonic ritornello at bar 219. The provisional form relation matches 9:31–9:48 with the opening ritornello; it does not establish an exact tutti entrance.

facts: Family musicians in Eisenach and Ohrdruf; school at Lüneburg; study of German, French and Italian scores
Arnstadt · Mühlhausen · Weimar · Köthen · Thomaskantor in Leipzig, 1723–50
Organ, harpsichord, clavichord and violin; an examiner of organs and a teacher of keyboard players
Cantatas, Passions, the B minor Mass, organ and keyboard cycles, concertos, unaccompanied string music
composer.background:
Bach was born into a family of professional musicians in Eisenach, where his father Johann Ambrosius served as a town musician. The surname already meant a trade: relatives supplied organists, cantors and instrumentalists across Thuringia. His mother died in 1694 and his father in 1695; at ten he went to live with his elder brother Johann Christoph, an organist in Ohrdruf who had studied with Pachelbel. Keyboard instruction belonged to that household, alongside school and choir. In 1700 Bach travelled to Lüneburg, where a place in the choir of St Michael’s school gave a boy without substantial means access to an education and a musical library.

The early career was practical and local. After a brief appointment at Weimar, he became organist of the New Church in Arnstadt in 1703, with a recently built instrument to test and play. His duties included working with students, and the town’s records preserve disputes over both his behaviour and his music. In 1705 he obtained leave to hear Dieterich Buxtehude in Lübeck and stayed away much longer than authorised. Buxtehude’s organ works offered a model in which free passagework, recurring basses and strict counterpoint could occupy the same piece. Bach’s own organ preludes would retain that alternation between improvisatory display and composed argument.
composer.epithet: An organist, teacher and church musician who made a bass line, a dance rhythm and a fugue subject carry the same argument.
